What Minnow is, what it is for, and how the docs are organized.

# Minnow

Minnow is a relational database that runs entirely in the browser: typed queries, real SQL, live results, and durable storage built on immutable compressed columnar blocks over IndexedDB.

There is no server, no WASM blob, and no build step. You declare a schema once, and that one declaration drives migrations, autocomplete, row types, typed writes with `returning`, and live subscriptions. Underneath sits an engine with MVCC snapshots, atomic multi-tab publication, vectorized execution with explicit memory budgets, and background compaction. ```ts import { createMinnow, MinnowDatabase, column, schema, table } from "@minnowdb/core"; import { IndexedDbBlockStore } from "@minnowdb/core/storage"; const people = table("people", { name: column.string().unique(), score: column.number(), joined: column.datetime().nullable(), }); const appSchema = schema([people]); const database = new MinnowDatabase(await IndexedDbBlockStore.open({ name: "app-db" })); await database.migrate(appSchema); const db = createMinnow(database, { schema: appSchema }); const rows = await db .selectFrom("people") .where("score", ">=", 10) .select(["name", "joined"]) .orderBy("name") .execute(); // Array<{ name: string; joined: Date | null }> ``` > Minnow is experimental. The version-zero block format carries no compatibility promise, and the > SQL surface is a correctness-first subset, not full SQL-92 coverage. ## Where to go - [Getting started](/docs/getting-started/) — install, first session, workers, testing. - [Best practices](/docs/best-practices/) — the patterns the engine is designed around. - [Schema & migrations](/docs/schema/) — the typed schema DSL and what `migrate()` will and won't do. - [Typed queries](/docs/queries/) — the Kysely-style builder and its expression vocabulary. - [Writes & transactions](/docs/writes/) — typed mutations, batch writes, buffered writers, maintenance. - [Live queries](/docs/live-queries/) — convergent re-execution when tables change. - [Workers & multi-tab](/docs/workers/) — the shipped worker entry and main-thread client. - [Architecture](/docs/architecture/) — storage model, MVCC, execution, fault model. - [API reference](/docs/api/) — every public export, by module. - [SQL support](/docs/sql/) — the checked-in feature matrix. - [Benchmarks](/benchmarks/) — measured against SQLite WASM and PGlite in real browsers. ## Design commitments A few properties are constraints on the project, not aspirations — the full list is in [Architecture](/docs/architecture/): - **IndexedDB is authoritative.** Correctness never depends on BroadcastChannel, Web Locks, page-close handlers, or successful background work. The durability contract ends at a successfully committed IndexedDB transaction. - **Published data is immutable.** Writes append compressed columnar segments and publish them with an atomic manifest compare-and-swap; another tab sees the old version or the new one, never a partial write. - **One plan, two front ends.** Builder queries compile to the exact plans their SQL equivalents produce, enforced by structural plan-equality tests. - **The engine is owned.** Parser, binder, planner, optimizer, and executor are implemented here — no SQLite, no DuckDB, no WASM engine underneath.

# Getting started

Minnow is a browser-only relational database built around immutable compressed columnar blocks and IndexedDB. It includes persistent writes and snapshots, a deliberately limited read-only SQL API with a columnar executor, resumable compaction, lease-aware garbage collection, and deterministic fault injection.

```bash npm install @minnowdb/core ``` > Experimental. The version-zero block format carries no compatibility promise, and the SQL surface > is a correctness-first subset, not full SQL-92 coverage. ## Logical types The public type system is intentionally small. A table column is one of: - `boolean` - `number` - `string` - `datetime` Numeric widths and physical encodings are storage details, not schema choices exposed to callers. Row IDs are assigned internally; callers do not choose an integer size. ## First session Declare a schema, open a block store, migrate, and work through the typed facade — one declaration drives migrations, autocomplete, row types, typed writes with `returning`, and [live queries](/docs/live-queries/): ```ts import { MinnowDatabase, Minnow, column, schema, table, type InferDatabase } from "@minnowdb/core"; import { IndexedDbBlockStore } from "@minnowdb/core/storage"; const people = table("people", { name: column.string().unique(), score: column.number(), joined: column.datetime().nullable(), }); const appSchema = schema([people]); const store = await IndexedDbBlockStore.open({ name: "app-db" }); const database = new MinnowDatabase(store); await database.migrate(appSchema); const db = new Minnow>(database, { schema: appSchema }); const written = await db .insertInto("people") .values([ { name: "Ada", score: 10, joined: new Date() }, { name: "Grace", score: 20 }, // joined pads to null ]) .returningAll() .execute(); const rows = await db .selectFrom("people") .where("score", ">=", 10) .select(["name", "joined"]) .orderBy("name") .execute(); // Array<{ name: string; joined: Date | null }> ``` Every write validates before it stores anything and publishes immutable columnar blocks through an atomic manifest compare-and-swap, so a reader in another tab sees either the old version or the new one, never a partial write. Builder queries compile to the exact plans their SQL equivalents produce — see [Typed queries](/docs/queries/). ## The SQL and batch layer Underneath the facade sit raw SQL and column-based batches — the layer the builders compile onto. Reach for it for bulk ingestion, ad-hoc SQL, or when compile-time types are not needed: ```ts await database.insertBatch("people", { columns: { name: ["Katherine", "Linus"], score: [30, 25], joined: [new Date(), null], }, }); const resultSet = await database.query(` SELECT score, COUNT(*) AS people FROM people WHERE score >= 20 GROUP BY score ORDER BY score DESC `); ``` Tables can also be created without the schema DSL via `createTable` — see [Writes & transactions](/docs/writes/). ## Run it in a worker `MinnowDatabase` runs wherever you construct it — the examples on the [home page](/) run it on the main thread against an in-memory store, and the calling code is identical either way because the public API is asynchronous throughout. For real datasets, run it in a dedicated worker: IndexedDB access, block decoding, and query execution are heavy enough to jank the main thread. The library ships both sides of that channel — `@minnowdb/core/worker` is a ready-made worker entry, and `MinnowDatabaseClient` (from `@minnowdb/core/client`) is a main-thread async proxy of the full API. Your application contributes one line — constructing the `Worker`: ```ts import { MinnowDatabaseClient } from "@minnowdb/core/client"; const client = new MinnowDatabaseClient( new Worker(new URL("@minnowdb/core/worker", import.meta.url), { type: "module" }), { store: { kind: "indexeddb", name: "app-db" } }, ); // Same code as above — the facade wraps the client exactly like a database: await client.migrate(appSchema); const db = new Minnow>(client, { schema: appSchema }); ``` See [Workers & multi-tab](/docs/workers/) for the full client API, bundler setups, and custom worker entries built on `exposeDatabase()`. > Correctness never depends on BroadcastChannel, Web Locks, page-close handlers, or successful > background work. IndexedDB is authoritative; the durability contract ends at a successfully > committed IndexedDB transaction. ## Testing with an in-memory store For unit tests, substitute a `MemoryBlockStore` for the IndexedDB store. It implements the same storage interface, so table creation, batch writes, queries, compaction, and garbage collection behave identically without touching real browser storage. ```ts import { MemoryBlockStore } from "@minnowdb/core/storage"; const database = new MinnowDatabase(new MemoryBlockStore()); ``` ## Where to go next - [Workers & multi-tab](/docs/workers/) — the worker entry and client. - [Writes & transactions](/docs/writes/) — batches, buffered writers, maintenance. - [Schema & migrations](/docs/schema/) — the typed schema DSL. - [Typed queries](/docs/queries/) — the Kysely-style typed API. - [Live queries](/docs/live-queries/) — convergent re-execution on change. - [Architecture](/docs/architecture/) — storage, MVCC, and execution model. - [SQL support](/docs/sql/) — the checked-in feature matrix.

# Typed queries

A Kysely-style typed query builder. String column references with autocomplete, an expression builder for everything beyond comparisons, and inferred row types — compiling to the same plans as SQL, never to SQL strings.

## Setup `Minnow` wraps a database (or the [worker client](/docs/workers/) — the API is identical over both). The `DB` type derives from the runtime schema, so one declaration drives migrations, autocomplete, and row types: ```ts import { Minnow, column, schema, table, type InferDatabase } from "@minnowdb/core"; const people = table("people", { name: column.string().unique(), score: column.number(), city: column.string().nullable(), }); const orders = table("orders", { order_id: column.number().unique(), person: column.string().references("people", "name"), total: column.number(), }); const appSchema = schema([people, orders]); await database.migrate(appSchema); const db = new Minnow>(database, { schema: appSchema }); ``` `createMinnow(database, { schema: appSchema })` does the same with the `DB` type inferred from the schema value — no generic passing. ## Selects ```ts const rows = await db .selectFrom("people as p") .innerJoin("orders as o", "o.person", "p.name") .where("p.score", ">", 10) .where((eb) => eb.or([eb("p.city", "=", "London"), eb("p.city", "is", null)])) .groupBy("p.name") .having((eb) => eb(eb.fn.countAll(), ">", 1)) .select(["p.name"]) .select((eb) => [eb.fn.sum("o.total").as("revenue")]) .orderBy("revenue", "desc") .limit(10) .execute(); // Array<{ name: string; revenue: number | null }> ``` - String left-hand sides are **column references**; right-hand sides are **values**. Compare two columns with `eb.ref("a.x")` or a join's `onRef`. - `select()` takes strings (`"p.name"`, `"p.name as owner"`), an expression callback, or both across repeated calls; `selectAll()` is `SELECT *`. - Left-joined columns widen to `| null` in the row type, matching what a left join actually returns. - `execute()`, `executeTakeFirst()`, `executeTakeFirstOrThrow()`, `compile()`, and [`.live()`](/docs/live-queries/). ## Expression vocabulary | Category | Forms | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Comparisons | `eb(lhs, op, rhs)` with `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `like`, `not like`, `in`, `not in`, `is`, `is not`; `eb.between`, `eb.notBetween` | | Boolean logic | `eb.and([...])`, `eb.or([...])`, `eb.not(...)` | | Arithmetic | `eb(lhs, "+" \| "-" \| "*" \| "/", rhs)`, `eb.neg(...)` | | Aggregates | `eb.fn.count`, `countAll`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`; `fn.count(x).distinct()` | | Scalar functions | `eb.fn.round`, `coalesce`, `dateTrunc` | | Windows | `eb.rowNumber() / rank() / denseRank()` and aggregate `.over((o) => o.partitionBy(...).orderBy(...))` | | Conditionals | `eb.case().when(...).then(...).else(...).end()` | | Subqueries | `eb.selectFrom(...)`, `eb.exists(...)`, and builders as `in` / comparison operands | Aggregate results are typed honestly: `sum` over an empty group is `null`, so its result type is `number | null`. ## Derived tables, CTEs, set operations ```ts const spend = db .selectFrom("orders") .groupBy("person") .select((eb) => [eb.ref("person").as("person"), eb.fn.sum("total").as("total")]); // As a derived table… await db.selectFrom(spend.as("t")).where("t.total", ">", 10).select(["t.person"]).execute(); // …or as a CTE, joinable by name. await db .with("spend", () => spend) .selectFrom("people as p") .innerJoin("spend", "spend.person", "p.name") .select(["p.name", "spend.total"]) .execute(); // Set operations chain left to right; member row types must match. await db .selectFrom("people") .select(["name"]) .unionAll(db.selectFrom("orders").select(["person as name"])) .orderBy("name") .execute(); ``` Derived and CTE columns stay fully type-checked — an unknown column on `"t."` is a compile error, exactly like a real table. ## One plan, two front ends `compile()` ends in the same assembly functions the SQL parser ends in, with a shared derived-source numbering sequence, so a builder query and its equivalent SQL produce _identical_ optimized plans — the same validation errors, the same DISTINCT/COUNT(DISTINCT)/window desugars, the same execution strategy. This is not an aspiration: structural plan-equality tests enforce it shape by shape. ``` SQL -> lexer -> parser ----------------+ +-> shared assembly -> optimizer -> physical plan Typed builder -> compile() ------------+ ``` ## The SQL escape hatch The `sql` template tag renders interpolations as SQL literals (strings escape their quotes, arrays become IN lists, nested fragments splice), and `query()` / `prepareQuery()` remain the raw read-only SQL API. Anything the builder does not express can be written as SQL against the same optimizer and executor. ```ts import { sql } from "@minnowdb/core"; const rows = await sql<{ n: number }>` SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM people WHERE city IN ${["London", "DC"]} `.execute(db); ``` > Writes have the same treatment — see [Writes & transactions](/docs/writes/) for `insertInto` / > `updateTable` / `deleteFrom` with `returning`. The supported and rejected SQL forms are recorded > in a checked-in feature matrix; see [SQL support](/docs/sql/), and > [live queries](/docs/live-queries/) for re-executing any built query when its tables change. > Known limits: correlated subqueries compile but the engine resolves subqueries at one snapshot, > so they fail at execution; ORDER BY must name a selected column or output alias.

# Schema & migrations

The schema DSL defines tables with compile-time row types and migrates the catalog through deterministic, metadata-only steps. No stored data is rewritten by a migration.

## Defining a schema ```ts import { Minnow, column, schema, table, type InferDatabase } from "@minnowdb/core"; const people = table("people", { name: column.string().unique(), score: column.number(), joined: column.datetime().nullable(), }); const appSchema = schema([people]); await database.migrate(appSchema); // The same declaration drives the query builder's types end to end: const db = new Minnow>(database, { schema: appSchema }); await db.insertInto("people").values({ name: "Ada", score: 10 }).execute(); // joined pads to null const rows = await db.selectFrom("people").selectAll().execute(); // Array<{ name: string; score: number; joined: Date | null }> ``` Column builders exist for the four logical types — `column.boolean()`, `column.number()`, `column.string()`, `column.datetime()` — with modifiers: - `.unique()` — marks the table's unique key (one non-null column). - `.nullable()` — permits NULL and widens the inferred type. - `.renamedFrom()` — renames a column through its stable ID, so a rename is a metadata step rather than a drop-and-add. - `.references()` — declares a relation. It validates at definition time and lives in catalog metadata; it is not enforced per write. ## Migration semantics `migrate()` diffs the live catalog into deterministic metadata-only steps: create table, add nullable column, rename through the stable column ID, widen nullability. Each catalog change executes with one atomic compare-and-swap, and the whole sequence is idempotent — an interrupted migration completes by re-running. A concurrent migrator fails with a typed conflict instead of interleaving. Rejected explicitly, rather than attempted: - type changes - column or table drops - unique-key changes - non-null tightening - non-nullable column additions Columns added after a segment was written read as NULL everywhere without rewriting stored data. Physical rewrites are deferred to [compaction](/docs/writes/) where possible. ## Inferred shapes `InferDatabase` maps table names to row types for `Minnow`. Lower-level helpers expose the per-table shapes (used by `typedTable()`, the thin schema-typed handle over the batch APIs): | Type | Meaning | | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | `InferRow` | The select shape; nullable columns are `\| null`. | | `InferInsertRow` | The insert shape; nullable columns may be omitted. | | `InferUpdateChanges` | The partial-update shape accepted by keyed updates. | Each table definition also carries a Standard Schema-compatible `~standard` validator, so a definition can be handed to any library that consumes the Standard Schema interface for runtime row validation. > The same definitions feed the [query builder](/docs/queries/) and the typed > [write API](/docs/writes/), which derive every reference and row type from these column > declarations. Raw `createTable` remains available when compile-time types are not needed.

# Live queries

Live queries re-execute selectively when their tables change. Re-execution is the correctness baseline; every notification path converges on the durable manifest version, so a missed message can delay a refresh but cannot produce a stale result.

## Typed live queries Any [built query](/docs/queries/) becomes a live query with `.live()`. Subscribers get the current typed rows immediately, then a fresh result after any commit that may have changed them; dependency tables come from the compiled plan, with no SQL re-parse. ```ts const live = db.selectFrom("people").select(["name"]).where("score", ">", 15).live(); const sub = await live.subscribe({ onChange: (rows) => render(rows), // rows: Array<{ name: string }> onComplete: () => {}, // optional: the live set closed }); // or, latest-wins async iteration: for await (const rows of live) render(rows); await sub.close(); await db.close(); // closes the shared live set; open iterators end cleanly ``` Iteration ends promptly on `break`, `iterator.return()` (so `Promise.race` timeouts work), or when the live set closes — a cancelled iterator never waits for the next commit. Async iteration coalesces to the latest result: every yielded value is a true snapshot, but a slow consumer may skip intermediates. Configure cross-tab hints and polling once, on the facade: `new Minnow(driver, { live: { channelName: "app-commits", pollIntervalMs: 5000 } })`. ## Subscribing with SQL The underlying live-query set also accepts raw SQL text: ```ts const live = database.liveQueries({ channelName: "db", pollIntervalMs: 5_000 }); const subscription = await live.subscribe( "SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status", { onChange: (result) => render(result) }, ); // later: subscription.close(); live.close(); ``` ## How convergence works Every commit persists its changed table IDs in the manifest before any notification (compaction marks itself logically unchanged). Four hint paths can trigger a sweep: - a local commit in the same database instance; - a cross-tab BroadcastChannel message; - a poll tick; - an explicit `refresh()`. All four converge on the same durable manifest version. Hints are only accelerants — the change sets in the manifest are authoritative, so missed messages and suspended tabs delay a refresh but cannot produce stale results. This matches the architectural rule that correctness never depends on BroadcastChannel delivery. ## Sweeps and suppression Sweeps read change sets in bounded pages and skip subscriptions whose tables did not change; a commit without a change set widens conservatively to every subscription. A subscription retains only its query (SQL text or compiled plan), its dependency table IDs, and a numeric result digest — never rows. When a rerun produces an unchanged digest, the notification is suppressed, so `onChange` fires only when the result actually differs. ## Observability `live.stats` reports counters for the mechanism itself: - hints received and sweeps performed; - reruns executed and reruns avoided by change-set filtering; - notifications suppressed by an unchanged digest; - sweep latency. ## Limitations > Incremental maintenance remains future work. When it arrives it will be introduced only for > proven-safe operator shapes, and full re-execution stays as the correctness baseline it is > checked against. Subscriptions accept anything the read surface executes — built queries or the > same read-only SQL subset as `query()`; see [SQL support](/docs/sql/). Related: [the query builder](/docs/queries/) compiles to the same plans these subscriptions execute (its `.live()` is this mechanism), and [Architecture](/docs/architecture/) covers manifests, change sets, and multi-tab coordination in more depth.

# Architecture

Minnow is a browser-only relational database engine for large local datasets, designed around immutable compressed columnar storage, asynchronous worker execution, and IndexedDB transactions. This page condenses the full ARCHITECTURE document.

## Architectural invariants These are constraints, not preferences: - Modern browsers only; database work never executes on the main thread. - No COOP/COEP requirement; no SharedArrayBuffer or Atomics dependency. - IndexedDB is the baseline persistence; OPFS may be added later behind the storage interface. - Published data is immutable compressed columnar blocks; writes are append-only delta segments, compacted asynchronously. - Snapshot isolation through versioned MVCC manifests; IndexedDB `relaxed` durability by default. - Vectorized query execution; streaming inputs, explicit memory budgets, and spill remain required exit gates. - Automatic statistics and data skipping; no user-managed indexes. - Correctness never depends on BroadcastChannel, Web Locks, page-close handlers, or successful background work. - The SQL parser, binder, planner, optimizer, and executor are owned by this project. SQLite, DuckDB, and other SQL engines are forbidden in the implementation. > The durability contract ends at a successfully committed IndexedDB transaction. Lifecycle signals > may request earlier flushing, but cannot make browser shutdown reliable. ## System shape In the target shape, the main thread holds only an async API proxy: request IDs, cancellation, and results — no encoding, storage, planning, or execution. Every tab owns a dedicated coordinator worker with catalog and snapshot ownership, transaction coordination, query planning, and live-query dependency tracking. Beneath it sit the storage modules (IndexedDB, block codecs, manifests, leases/GC) and, later, executor workers for segment-grained tasks. Buffers cross worker boundaries as transferable `ArrayBuffer`s; parallelism is coarse-grained by immutable segment, so no shared queue or shared buffer cache is needed. > Today the library ships the engine, the versioned wire protocol, the worker entry, and the > main-thread full-API proxy (`MinnowDatabaseClient`) — see [Workers & multi-tab](/docs/workers/). > Not shipped yet from the target shape: executor workers beneath the coordinator for > segment-grained parallelism. Inside `@minnowdb/core` the layers map onto modules: `block-format` (versioned binary containers, statistics, codecs), `storage` (IndexedDB block and metadata persistence), `transactions` (snapshots, journals, atomic commits, recovery), and the engine (the coordinator and public API). Each is importable directly — `@minnowdb/core/block-format`, `@minnowdb/core/storage`, `@minnowdb/core/transactions`. ## Logical and physical storage ``` Database -> Table -> Segment -> Row group -> Column block ``` - A segment is the immutable visibility and compaction unit. - A row group is the primary pruning and vector-scan unit. - A column block contains one encoded logical column for one row group. - Inserts, updates, and deletes land first in append-only L0 deltas; compaction rewrites them into larger query-oriented segments. No row is stored as an individual IndexedDB value, and no entire table is one giant value. Every block starts with a fixed little-endian header: magic bytes, format version, type and encoding IDs, codec ID, row and null counts, payload lengths, a checksum of the uncompressed encoded payload, and optional zone-map statistics. Readers reject unknown mandatory versions, invalid lengths, unsupported codecs, and checksum mismatches. Published formats are append-only: new codecs use new IDs rather than changing old bytes. ## MVCC and atomic publication Each transaction records a transaction ID, snapshot manifest version, pending blocks, and a compact change set. Readers resolve all data through one immutable manifest. Commit encodes and persists immutable blocks first, then opens a short IndexedDB metadata transaction, compares the expected manifest version, and publishes manifest N + 1. The manifest never references a partial block; a crash before publication leaves only unreachable blocks for later garbage collection. A compare-and-swap failure is a normal write conflict — the caller rebases or retries. Tables carry a hidden immutable row ID; writers atomically reserve ranges. Inserts create immutable column segments, upserts create newer keyed segments, partial updates create narrow key-plus-changed-columns segments, and deletes create key-only markers. Compaction uses the same atomic publication path and preserves row identity through ordered `rowIdSpans`; it rebases across concurrent commits while its sources remain visible, and aborts rather than publishing a stale rewrite. ## Multi-tab correctness IndexedDB is authoritative. The final metadata transaction serializes manifest publication across tabs and workers; the compare-and-swap in IndexedDB is the correctness mechanism. BroadcastChannel may announce that a new version exists, but receivers always reconcile against IndexedDB, so missed or duplicated announcements are harmless. Reader and backup leases are persistent records with expiry — not inferred from open channels — and garbage collection retains everything an unexpired lease, active transaction, or active compaction still reaches. ## Vectorized execution and bounded memory Queries execute over typed vectors: booleans as bytes, numbers and datetimes as `Float64Array`, strings dictionary-coded, each with a packed validity bitmap. The executor scans 2,048 source rows per batch. Queries accept an explicit `executionMemoryBudgetBytes`: retained vectors, join indexes, and grouped state reserve bytes before allocation, and a reservation exceeding the budget throws `QueryMemoryBudgetError`. Under a budget, ordered plans use asynchronous external merge sort and grouped plans use 64-way partitioned hash aggregation, spilling to durable lease-protected temp pages; a narrow plan family also streams its scan input through a sliding block-aligned window. > The bounded-memory exit gate is not yet claimed. Non-streamed shapes still materialize projected > columns in full, hash-join build sides have no spill path, and the model excludes result objects, > JavaScript array overhead, and browser allocator overhead. The figures are modeled workflow > bounds, not hard heap limits. ## Automatic data skipping Block zone maps (row count, null count, numeric/datetime min/max) provide a conservative scan fast path for a single append/base table with AND-combined column-to-literal predicates: impossible row groups are rejected before vector materialization. Predicate blocks are checksum-verified and physically decoded before their metadata is trusted, because version-zero metadata has no independent checksum. Joins, mutation snapshots, strings, and computed predicates retain the full scan. Derived statistics are disposable; logical correctness never depends on them. ## Fault model Deterministic fault injection has been required from the first storage implementation, with named points before and after block writes and manifest commits. The suite covers abandoned writers, stale tabs, corrupted bytes, transaction aborts, and crashes between block persistence and manifest publication. The core invariants under faults: 1. A visible manifest references only complete, checksum-valid blocks. 2. A failed or stale manifest comparison cannot publish changes. 3. Retrying an immutable block write cannot mutate already-published bytes. 4. Unpublished objects never affect reads and are safe to collect later. 5. UI responsiveness does not depend on operation size. ## Explicit non-goals - No full SQL surface yet; the current subset is deliberately limited, and its executor does not claim the bounded-memory exit gate. - No claim of multi-gigabyte performance until browser measurements support it. - No required OPFS, Web Locks, BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker, WASM, or SharedArrayBuffer. - No user-facing index DDL. - No compatibility promise for the experimental version-zero block format. See [Getting started](/docs/getting-started/) for the API entry point, [Writes & transactions](/docs/writes/) for compaction and garbage collection details, and [Benchmarks](/benchmarks/) for the measurements behind the decision gates.

# Best practices

Minnow has opinions. Most of them exist so that the failure you see in development is the same one you would have seen in production — this page collects the patterns the engine is designed around and the traps it deliberately refuses to paper over.

## Run the database in a worker The engine runs wherever you construct it, but IndexedDB access, block decoding, planning, and query execution are heavy enough to jank the main thread. In production, construct the database in a dedicated worker and keep only the proxy on the main thread — the shipped [worker entry and client](/docs/workers/) make this a three-line setup, and the typed facade behaves identically over both. Reserve main-thread construction for tests and prototypes. ## Declare the schema once, work typed One `schema([...])` declaration drives migrations, autocomplete, row types, typed writes, and live queries. Prefer `createMinnow(database, { schema })` — it infers the `DB` type from the schema value, so there is no generic to keep in sync: ```ts const db = createMinnow(database, { schema: appSchema }); ``` Drop to the raw layer (`database.query()`, `insertBatch()`, the `sql` tag) for bulk ingestion and ad-hoc SQL — it is the same pipeline, not a second engine. Builder queries compile to the exact plans their SQL equivalents produce, so switching layers never changes semantics. ## Write in batches, not loops Every commit publishes segments and runs a manifest compare-and-swap; a loop of single-row inserts pays that full cost per row. Give the engine columns, or let the buffered writer do the batching: ```ts // Bulk load: one commit, columnar from the start. await database.insertBatch("events", { columns: { id: ids, at: dates, kind: kinds } }); // Event streams: rows in, batches out. const writer = database.bufferedWriter("events", { mode: "upsert", maxRows: 1_000, maxAgeMs: 1_000, onError: (error) => report(error), }); await writer.add(event); ``` ## Do not trust page unload `attachLifecycleFlush()` flushes buffered writers when the tab hides — use it, but treat it as an optimization. The durability contract ends at a successfully committed IndexedDB transaction; nothing you do in `pagehide` makes browser shutdown reliable. Data that must survive belongs in a committed batch, not in a buffer you hope will flush. ## Give big queries a memory budget Queries accept `executionMemoryBudgetBytes`. Without one, a large sort or join materializes what it needs and may take the tab down with it; with one, ordered plans switch to external merge sort and grouped plans to partitioned spill, or you get a typed `QueryMemoryBudgetError` instead of a crashed tab: ```ts try { const result = await database.query(bigSql, { executionMemoryBudgetBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024 }); } catch (error) { if (error instanceof QueryMemoryBudgetError) { // narrow the query, raise the budget, or page through smaller slices } } ``` If a tab can die abruptly mid-query, schedule `cleanupQuerySpill()` occasionally so abandoned spill pages are reclaimed once their owner leases expire. ## Expect write conflicts; handle them as data Concurrent tabs are a designed-for case, and the resolution is explicit: a losing commit fails its manifest compare-and-swap and surfaces a typed error rather than interleaving. Catch `UniqueConstraintError` / conflict failures and retry or rebase at the level where you know what the right merge is. The engine retries transparently where that is safe (`maxCommitRetries`); what reaches you is the case that genuinely needs an application decision. ## Treat migrations as additive `migrate()` performs metadata-only steps and rejects everything destructive: type changes, drops, unique-key changes, non-null tightening. Design schemas accordingly — add nullable columns, rename through `.renamedFrom()` (a metadata step, not a drop-and-add), and let [compaction](/docs/writes/) handle physical rewrites. If a truly breaking change is unavoidable, that is a new table plus an application-level copy, done deliberately. ## Close what you open `prepareQuery()` pins an immutable snapshot until `close()` — a leaked prepared query pins history and blocks garbage collection from reclaiming it. Live subscriptions, buffered writers, live sets, and the database itself all have `close()`; on the worker client, `close({ terminateWorker: true })` tears down the whole stack cleanly. ## Schedule maintenance in idle time Compaction, garbage collection, and spill cleanup are stepped, durable, and cancellable — designed to run in small increments whenever the app is quiet, and to survive a tab closing mid-job: ```ts requestIdleCallback(async () => { await database.compactTableStep("events", { maxBlocks: 1 }); await database.collectGarbageStep({ maxItems: 8 }); }); ``` A resumed job continues from its durable checkpoint; there is no penalty for stopping. ## Test against the same engine `MemoryBlockStore` implements the full storage interface, so unit tests run the real engine — planner, executor, compaction, GC — without touching browser storage. For crash and recovery testing, `FaultInjectingBlockStore` (from `@minnowdb/core/testing`) injects deterministic faults at named points around block writes and manifest commits: ```ts import { MemoryBlockStore } from "@minnowdb/core/storage"; import { FaultInjectingBlockStore } from "@minnowdb/core/testing"; const store = new FaultInjectingBlockStore(new MemoryBlockStore(), (point) => { if (point === "beforeManifestCommit") throw new Error("crash here"); }); ``` If your test would pass against a mock but fail against the engine, the engine was telling you something.
